intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that auriculocondylar syndrome-4 (ARCND4) is caused by a tandem duplication on chromosome 7p21.1 that covers most of the HDAC9 gene (606543) and is thought to contain TWIST1 regulatory elements.

checks.evidence_quote: This study highlights a fourth locus causative of ARCND, represented by a tandem duplication of 430 kb in a candidate region on chromosome 7 defined by linkage analysis.
checks.explanation: 7p21.1 is standard location for HDAC9 region.

checks.claim: The ARCND4-associated tandem duplication on chromosome 7p21.1 covers most of the HDAC9 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: The duplication spanned 430 302 bp (NC_000007.14:g.18437239_18867540dup) telomeric to TWIST1, covering most of the HDAC9 gene.

checks.claim: The ARCND4-associated tandem duplication on chromosome 7p21.1 is thought to contain TWIST1 regulatory elements.
checks.evidence_quote: New locus underlying auriculocondylar syndrome (ARCND): 430 kb duplication involving TWIST1 regulatory elements.

paragraphs.text: Auriculocondylar syndrome is characterized by malformed 'question mark' ears, prominent cheeks, microstomia, an abnormal temporomandibular joint, and hypoplasia of the mandibular condyle (Masotti et al., 2008). Features vary considerably within families, and micrognathia and facial asymmetry are also reported (Masotti et al., 2008; Romanelli Tavares et al., 2022).

Most of the patients had facial asymmetry. The authors noted that earlier reports of auriculocondylar syndrome had not highlighted this feature.

paragraphs.text: Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) studied a previously reported nonconsanguineous 4-generation Brazilian family in which 11 members had typical features of auriculocondylar syndrome. Ten affected members were documented. Of these, 8 had question mark ears, 8 had microstomia, and 6 had micrognathia, and features varied considerably within the family. None of the patients had large, open fontanelles, which are the hallmark of trisomy 7p.

paragraphs.text: Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) identified 19 patients in the DECIPHER database with copy-number gains in the region. Seven had ear malformations and 7 had micrognathia. Most of these patients had larger duplications that included the TWIST1 enhancer eTW6. One 179-kb duplication (patient 276644) lay entirely within the region duplicated in the ARCND family but did not span the TWIST1 regulatory elements. This duplication was not associated with ARCND features.

paragraphs.text: Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) studied a Brazilian family with auriculocondylar syndrome in which Sanger sequencing of the PLCB4, GNAI3, and EDN1 genes had found no pathogenic variants. They performed genomewide SNP linkage analysis in 9 affected and 3 unaffected family members under an autosomal dominant model. They found a maximum lod score of 2.88 (maximum theoretical 2.93) in a 17.6-Mb region on chromosome 7 (chr7:14,395,902-32,017,194, hg38). Microsatellite markers narrowed the region to chr7:14,395,902-28,158,440. Gene prioritization ranked TWIST1 as the top candidate gene in the region.

paragraphs.text: Masotti et al. (2008) performed linkage analysis in 2 large families with auriculocondylar syndrome, F1 and F2. Segregation analysis excluded the loci for Treacher Collins syndrome, oculoauriculovertebral spectrum, and Townes-Brocks syndrome. A genomewide search found evidence of linkage to 1p21.1-q23.3 in family F2 (maximum lod score of 3.01 at theta = 0), which defined the first ACS locus. This locus was not linked to the phenotype in family F1. The authors concluded that auriculocondylar syndrome is genetically heterogeneous, with at least 2 loci responsible for the phenotype.

paragraphs.text: In the Brazilian family with ARCND4, Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) found no causative variants by whole-exome sequencing of 4 affected members; a synonymous variant in the TRIL gene did not segregate with the disorder. Targeted resequencing of a 2.4-Mb region around TWIST1 identified a 430,302-bp tandem duplication (NC_000007.14:g.18437239_18867540dup). The duplication began about 280 kb telomeric to TWIST1 and covered most of the HDAC9 gene. Breakpoint PCR and Sanger sequencing showed that the duplication segregated with the phenotype. All unaffected individuals were negative for the duplication, suggesting full penetrance. The duplication was predicted to disrupt the full-length, catalytically active HDAC9 isoforms.

paragraphs.text: Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) performed Capture-C analysis in human embryonic calvarial mesenchymal cells, using the TWIST1 promoter as the viewpoint. This showed multiple cis contacts, with the highest frequency of contacts telomeric to TWIST1, within HDAC9 and the duplicated region. These results implied that the duplicated region contains TWIST1 regulatory elements, including the enhancer eTw6, and suggested a possible pathogenic mechanism.

paragraphs.text: Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) generated induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) from 3 affected family members and from controls. They differentiated these cells into neural crest cells (iNCCs) and mesenchymal stem-like cells (nMSCs). Compared with controls, patient iNCCs had increased mRNA levels of HDAC9 (3.15-fold) and TWIST1 (2.03-fold) and a 4.3-fold decrease in migratory capacity, with no difference in the cell cycle. Patient nMSCs had reduced alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity (a 20.3-fold decrease), reduced ALP expression, and subtly reduced matrix mineralization, indicating delayed or impaired osteogenic differentiation. The authors suggested that deregulation of TWIST1 contributes to ARCND by compromising neural crest cell migration and osteogenesis.

paragraphs.text: In affected members of a nonconsanguineous 4-generation Brazilian family with auriculocondylar syndrome-4, Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) identified a 430,302-bp tandem duplication (NC_000007.14:g.18437239_18867540dup) on chromosome 7p21.1. They found it by targeted resequencing of a 2.4-Mb region around TWIST1 after whole-exome sequencing had found no causative variants. The duplication began about 280 kb telomeric to TWIST1 and covered most of the HDAC9 gene. Breakpoint PCR and Sanger sequencing showed segregation with the phenotype, and all unaffected family members were negative. The duplication was predicted to disrupt the full-length, catalytically active HDAC9 isoforms. Capture-C analysis showed that the duplicated region contacts the TWIST1 promoter. Neural crest cells derived from patient iPSCs had increased HDAC9 and TWIST1 expression and reduced migration.
